accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters 2021 (3-4 year olds: show finger numbers up to 5; Reception: subitise and explore the composition of numbers to 10), NCETM early-years guidance on '5 and a bit' for 6-10 on two hands, and Common Core K.CC.B.4 and K.CC.B.5. Counting each raised finger once is one-to-one correspondence and the last-number-said rule is the cardinal principle, both stated correctly.

misconceptions.evidence: Wrong moves name real early-counting slips: counting a finger twice or skipping one, thinking the count changes if you start from the little finger instead of the thumb, trying to show 7 on one hand, raising 8 fingers for 3 more than 5, and counting folded fingers. The adult text flags the grown-up slip of always counting from 1 instead of seeing a full hand as 5.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfing draws two cartoon hands where each finger is raised or folded by touch; steps cover showing a number, touch-counting the raised fingers, 5 and some more across two hands, three ways to make 5, and a five-little-ducks fold-down song. flagcount moves loose objects for one-to-one counting and never uses hands or composition of 5; the shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Raising one finger too many is answered at once with the exact count ('Only 1 more went up. 3, then 4. Not 5.'), and on the bigger-than-5 step a single hand runs out at 5 fingers, so the child discovers the second hand is needed before the text names 5 and some more.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions: whether counting from the little finger gives a different number (many 3-4 year olds think so), whether 7 fits on one hand, and how many 3 fingers and 2 fingers make. Each is tested by the very next task and the done message quotes the child's own guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The quiz rotates finger pictures and story prompts (age on fingers, two hands of 2) with tagged wrong answers: counted folded fingers, counted one twice, read the first not the last number said, and added hands wrongly. Each tag gives its own one-line correction and the draw step reminds the child to use their own fingers.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores FK -0.7 against the family limit of 5.0, written in two- to eight-word sentences such as 'Hold up 3 fingers.' Adult text scores FK 6.8 against 10 while using the terms finger numbers, subitising, one-to-one correspondence, cardinal principle, composition of 5 and '5 and a bit'.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed with no stock phrases. Every kid paragraph carries an action the child can do with their own hand right away, and each adult paragraph gives curriculum, method, named mistakes or a description of the lab; explanation overlap with other lessons stays under 12 percent.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 (iPhone class) in light and dark show both hands sized to fill the stage with the thumb clear of the palm, the ducks row fitting cleanly, and the Up/Down/Check buttons wrapping below the canvas. walk.cjs ran every Show me on desktop and iPhone 13 inside the 6 s limit.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme on desktop or iPhone, with no console errors. Every gesture has a button twin with a spoken label such as 'Left hand: one more finger up', 'Touch the next finger' and 'Check my fingers', and the canvas aria-label announces the current count.

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: mathematics (3-4 year olds and Reception)
NCETM Early Years: subitising and finger numbers, '5 and a bit'
Common Core State Standards Mathematics K.CC.B.4, K.CC.B.5
